title: How we turned one Aseprite kobold into 100 variants without redrawing its animations
author: Excellent_Divide_154
selftext:
We built SpriteRelay, a tool that lets an AI assistant edit Aseprite files. For this experiment, we used Claude to build one 64×64 kobold. The interesting part was deciding what needed its own animation and what could share one.

The master file has 43 frames. The kobold can carry a club, spear, bow or staff, so it needs four different attacks. Changing its helmet or turning its scales blue, on the other hand, doesn’t change how it swings a club.

We split the export into two steps:

1. Pick a head and weapon. Strip out the unused layers, attack frames, tags and hitboxes. That gives us 20 gear combinations, each with a 25-frame animation set.
2. Export each combination with five indexed palettes. A frost spear kobold and an ember spear kobold use the same animation timing. Only the colours change.

That’s where the 100 comes from: five heads × four weapons × five palettes. If you want to see what actually changes, pick a kobold, play its attack, then switch **only the weapon**. The [browser demo](https://www.spriterelay.com/play/enemy-forge/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) shows the exported frames, timings and hitbox data for that combination.

For anyone who’s shipped enemies like this: would you keep a separate sprite sheet per loadout, or assemble the gear and apply the palette in-engine? I’d be interested in what drove that choice in your game.

comments.author: Koden02
comments.body:
Personally, I'd handle this in-engine in Godot. You can use palette-swapping shaders for colors and keep weapons and other interchangeable parts on separate sprite layers synced to the animations.

Generating a new spritesheet for every combination seems like it could become a maintenance headache as you add more variants. I can see the value in automating the exports, though! Especially if it starts as a placeholder and you just swap it out later.
